idiom_name: row object with its own CRUD methods (structure is language-neutral)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one class per table whose fields are the columns and whose instances are rows, then give it (a) lookup functions that build instances from rows, (b) create/save/update/delete operations that write the instance back, and (c) the domain behaviour that belongs to that single row. The mapping is carried by convention or a small declarative mapping (name, primary key, column attributes) instead of a separate mapper object, and a version or timestamp column is what makes concurrent updates detectable. Keep the pattern honest: one class per table, domain rules that concern one row, and an explicit transaction around anything that must be atomic across several saves.
code_sketch:
record = Record.find(id)     # SELECT -> object holding data + logic
record.field = "new"
record.save()                # UPDATE (INSERT when the object is new)
record.delete()              # DELETE ... WHERE id = record.id
# finders stay row-shaped: Record.find / Record.where(...)
pitfalls: Letting the object grow cross-row workflow: the moment a save touches several tables as one unit of logic, the pattern has been outgrown.
Persisting a partially loaded instance writes defaults over columns that were never read; know whether an instance is new, loaded or a stub before saving.
No transaction around logically coupled saves leaves the database in a state no single object can repair.
Wrong move: call save() on a partially loaded record; it writes defaults or stale columns and erases concurrent edits; instead load the full row or issue a narrow update with optimistic locking.

Wrong move: put a multi-record workflow in callbacks or record methods; it hides the transaction boundary and can leave half-committed state; instead orchestrate it in a service or Unit of Work with one explicit transaction.
Wrong move: traverse lazy associations in a loop; it emits one query per record and collapses under load; instead shape one eager-loaded query or a column projection.
